newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Norway's Dyno launches profits programme.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Norway's Dyno launches profits programme.

text.p: Norway's Dyno Industrier ASA unveiled a programme for boosting profits by the year 2000 on Friday after booking a first-quarter pre-tax result of 93 million crowns ($13.1 million).

The company, one of the world's largest manufacturers of commercial explosives, attributed the 7.5 percent improvement in pre-tax profits on the corresponding 1996 period to better results in the explosives and chemicals businesses.
But the plastics division suffered a major setback in part because the strong Norwegian crown narrowed its export profit margins.
Group operating revenue rose to 2.55 billion crowns from 2.28 billion in the first quarter of 1996 while the operating profit fell to 102 million from 117 million.
The results largerly met market expectations.

Dyno said it hoped to achieve annual operating profits of a minimum 1.0 billion crowns by the year 2000 under the so-called "Dyno 2000" improvement programme. Dyno's 1996 operating profit was 460 million crowns, down 24 percent from the corresponding 1995 period.
"Today's international world places new and greater demands on companies," outgoing president Arild Ingierd wrote in the Inside Dyno in-house magazine, which accompanied the results.
"No silver medals are awarded in this competition -- you either win a contract or you don't," he said.

The improvement programme, to be executed under new president Dag Mejdell, aims to reach a return on capital employed of 16 percent by the year 2000. The programme will not start having an effect until in 1998, Dyno said.
"This sounds very ambitious," an Oslo-based analyst said. "Dyno has been criticised because profits have been too low, and this is why they have been working on this programme."
A Dyno statement said: "The programme comprises specific plans and measures within all parts of Dyno to increase productivity and sales volumes and reduce costs."

The first quarter saw the explosives division increase its operating profit by two million crowns to 50 million. General market conditions for explosives are good and developing in line with company plans, Dyno said.
The chemicals operating profit rose to 72 million from 53 million thanks to an increase in sales volumes and a rise in methanol prices.

But plastics's operating profit shrank to seven million crowns from 31 million in the first quarter of 1996. The result was blamed on lower market demand for industrial packaging and transport systems.
"In addition prices of important raw materials have been rising and a strong Norwegian crown has weakened margins for those units exporting plastic products from Norway," Dyno said.
The company said it expected the economic situation in most of it's main markets to remain relatively unchanged this year.

"However, a rise in interest rates in the United States and Europe could lead to a fall in demand for Dyno's products from the construction and civil engineering sector, wood processing industry and chemicals industry," Dyno said.
